title: Coffee Panna Cotta
subtitle: Set espresso cream with a silky, barely-wobbling texture
excerpt: Cream set with just enough gelatine to unmould cleanly, flavoured with real espresso for a clean, sharp coffee note. Chill for at least 4 hours before turning out.
sourceNotes: Panna cotta is a northern Italian dessert whose name means 'cooked cream'. It became a fixture of British restaurant menus in the 1990s and has since settled into home cooking as a reliable, make-ahead dessert requiring no baking. The coffee version uses espresso for a stronger flavour than the plain vanilla original.

recipe.batchNotes: Can be made up to 2 days ahead and kept refrigerated in the moulds until needed.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the day before and refrigerate in the moulds overnight. Turn out just before serving.

content.text: Coffee panna cotta is set cream flavoured with real espresso, turned out of the mould to reveal a smooth, barely-trembling dome with a deep coffee colour. The gelatine gives just enough structure to hold the shape while the cream stays silky and yielding inside. The espresso should be fresh and strong, filter or instant coffee gives a flat, muddy flavour by comparison. Chill for at least 4 hours, or leave overnight for a firmer set.

Submerge the gelatine leaves in a bowl of cold water and leave for 5 minutes until they are soft and pliable. Lightly brush the insides of 4 to 6 ramekins with a neutral oil, just enough to help release the set cream cleanly.

Pour the double cream into a small saucepan with the caster sugar. Heat over a medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the sugar has dissolved and the cream is just about to boil, you will see small bubbles forming around the edge. Do not let it reach a full rolling boil. Remove from the heat. Lift the gelatine leaves from the water, squeeze out the excess, and drop them into the hot cream. Stir until completely dissolved. Add the vanilla extract and the espresso, and stir to combine.

Pour the coffee cream mixture through a fine sieve into a jug, then divide evenly between the prepared ramekins. Leave to cool to room temperature, then cover with cling film and refrigerate for at least 4 hours until set. To unmould, run a thin knife around the inside edge of each ramekin, place a plate over the top, and invert firmly. The panna cotta should slide out cleanly. If it sticks, dip the base of the ramekin briefly in warm water for 10 seconds and try again.

items.cause: The gelatine was not fully dissolved, or too little was used.
items.fix: Check the gelatine was completely dissolved before pouring, hold the pan to a light to look for undissolved strands. Next time, increase to 3.5 sheets for a firmer result.

items.cause: Too much gelatine, or the mixture was chilled for too long at a very cold temperature.
items.fix: Reduce to 2.5 sheets next time. Panna cotta should wobble noticeably when the mould is nudged.

items.cause: The espresso shots were small or under-extracted.
items.fix: Use two full, properly extracted espresso shots (about 60ml total). For an even stronger result, reduce the espresso by simmering it briefly in a small pan, then add.

content.text: Keeps in the moulds, covered, in the fridge for up to 2 days. Once unmoulded, serve within 30 minutes. Do not freeze.
